output.answer: EM measures the percentage of predictions that exactly match any one ground-truth answer; F1 measures macro-averaged token-bag overlap, taking the maximum F1 over the ground-truth answers for each question and then averaging over questions. In SQuAD 2.0, a correct abstention scores 1 and any nonempty answer scores 0 on both EM and F1. The no-answer threshold is tuned separately for each model on the development set, choosing the value that maximizes development-set F1, and that threshold is used for test evaluation.

citations.claim: SQuAD's Exact Match measures the percentage of predictions that exactly match any one ground-truth answer.
citations.quote: Exact match. This metric measures the percentage of predictions that match any one of the ground truth answers exactly.

citations.claim: SQuAD's F1 treats prediction and ground truth as bags of tokens, takes the maximum F1 over all ground-truth answers for a question, and averages over questions.
citations.quote: (Macro-averaged) F1 score. This metric measures the average overlap between the prediction and ground truth answer. We treat the prediction and ground truth as bags of tokens, and compute their F1. We take the maximum F1 over all of the ground truth answers for a given question, and then average over all of the questions.

citations.claim: For SQuAD 2.0 negative examples, abstaining scores 1 and any other response scores 0 for both exact match and F1.
citations.quote: For negative examples, abstaining receives a score of 1, and any other response gets 0, for both exact match and F1.

citations.claim: The no-answer threshold is tuned separately for each model on the development set, and test evaluation uses the threshold that maximizes development-set F1.
citations.quote: We tune this threshold separately for each model on the development set. When evaluating on the test set, we use the threshold that maximizes F1 score on the development set.

output.answer: ResNet’s identity block adds the shortcut to the residual branch element-wise (F(x)+x); DenseNet concatenates instead, so each layer receives all preceding feature-maps in its dense block (x0,…,xℓ−1). Consequently, DenseNet’s input channel count grows with depth (k0+k(ℓ−1)), whereas the identity-shortcut addition requires matching dimensions.

citations.claim: ResNet’s identity shortcut performs identity mapping, and its output is added to the stacked-layer outputs.
citations.quote: In our case, the shortcut connections simply perform identity mapping, and their outputs are added to the outputs of the stacked layers (Fig. 2).

citations.claim: The addition in ResNet’s identity block is element-wise.
citations.quote: The operation F + x is performed by a shortcut connection and element-wise addition.

citations.claim: DenseNet combines features by concatenation rather than summation.
citations.quote: Crucially, in contrast to ResNets, we never combine features through summation before they are passed into a layer; instead, we combine features by concatenating them.

citations.claim: A DenseNet layer receives the feature-maps of all preceding layers as input.
citations.quote: the ℓth layer receives the feature-maps of all preceding layers, x0, . . . , xℓ−1, as input

citations.claim: Those inputs are concatenated feature-maps from layers 0 through ℓ−1.
citations.quote: where [x0, x1, . . . , xℓ−1] refers to the concatenation of the feature-maps produced in layers 0, . . . , ℓ−1.

citations.claim: Within a dense block, each layer has access to all preceding feature-maps in its block.
citations.quote: each layer has access to all the preceding feature-maps in its block

citations.claim: DenseNet’s ℓth layer has k0 + k(ℓ−1) input feature-maps.
citations.quote: the ℓth layer has k0 +k ×(ℓ−1) input feature-maps

citations.claim: ResNet’s identity-shortcut equation requires x and F to have equal dimensions.
citations.quote: The dimensions of x and F must be equal in Eqn.(1).

output.answer: ResNet: 3.57% top-5 error for its six-model ILSVRC'15 ensemble on the 100k-image ImageNet test set, reported by the test server. DenseNet-201: 6.34% single-crop and 5.54% 10-crop top-5 error on the 50k-image ImageNet validation set, using the DenseNet-BC-201 model, 224×224 crops, and the same Torch settings as its ResNet comparison. No—the ResNet figure is a test-set ensemble result, while the DenseNet figures are validation single-model single/10-crop results, so they do not establish a like-for-like head-to-head advantage.

output.answer: ViT prepends a learnable class token to the patch tokens, and its final encoder output is the image representation used by the classification head to predict the class. In DeiT's distillation-token procedure, the class branch is trained on the true (ground-truth) label, while the distillation branch is trained on the teacher's hard predicted label; late fusion adds the softmax outputs of the two separate classifiers to make the prediction.

citations.claim: ViT performs classification by adding an extra learnable classification token to the sequence.
citations.quote: In order to perform classification, we use the standard approach of adding an extra learnable “classification token” to the sequence.

citations.claim: The class token is prepended to the embedded patches, and its state at the encoder output is the image representation to which the classification head is attached.
citations.quote: Similar to BERT’s [class] token, we prepend a learnable embedding to the sequence of embedded patches (z0 0 = xclass), whose state at the output of the Transformer encoder (z0 L) serves as the image representation y (Eq. 4). Both during pre-training and fine-tuning, a classification head is attached to z0 L.

citations.claim: In DeiT, the class token is a trainable vector appended to the patch tokens that goes through the transformer and is linearly projected to predict the class.
citations.quote: The class token is a trainable vector, appended to the patch tokens before the first layer, that goes through the transformer layers, and is then projected with a linear layer to predict the class.

citations.claim: The distillation token reproduces the hard label predicted by the teacher instead of the true label.
citations.quote: This distillation token is employed in a similar fashion as the class token, except that on output of the network its objective is to reproduce the (hard) label predicted by the teacher, instead of true label.

citations.claim: The distillation token's target is the distillation component of the loss.
citations.quote: Its target objective is given by the distillation component of the loss.

citations.claim: Both the true label and the teacher prediction are used during fine-tuning.
citations.quote: We use both the true label and teacher prediction during the fine-tuning stage at higher resolution.

citations.claim: Late fusion adds the softmax outputs of the two separate classifiers to make the prediction.
citations.quote: Yet our referent method is the late fusion of these two separate heads, for which we add the softmax output by the two classifiers to make the prediction.

citations.claim: The class+distillation result corresponds to late fusion of the class and distillation classifiers.
citations.quote: In the last row (class+distillation), the result correspond to the late fusion of the class and distillation classifiers.

output.explanation: ViT follows BERT in prepending an extra learnable classification token to the sequence of patch embeddings; the state of that token at the output of the Transformer encoder serves as the image representation y, and a classification head is attached to it during both pre-training and fine-tuning (2010.11929v2.pdf, page 3). DeiT describes the same class token as a trainable vector appended before the first layer that passes through the transformer layers and is projected by a linear layer to predict the class; only this class embedding receives the supervision signal, while patch tokens are the variable input (2012.12877v2.pdf, page 5). DeiT then adds a distillation token used like the class token through self-attention, except that its output objective is to reproduce the hard label predicted by the teacher instead of the true label; its target is the distillation component of the loss (page 7). Both the true label and the teacher prediction are used in training/fine-tuning (page 8). The referent late-fusion inference associates the class and distillation embeddings each with a linear classifier and adds the softmax outputs of the two classifiers to make the prediction (page 8), which Table 3's class+distillation row identifies as late fusion (page 10). Limitation: the papers do not state per-branch loss weights in the requested level of detail beyond saying the class branch uses the true label and the distillation branch uses the teacher's hard label (hard-label distillation is y_t = argmax_c Z_t(c), page 6).

citations.claim: Relative entity frequency also compares an entity's frequency with the frequency of its co-occurring mentions, normalized by the sum of other entities' frequencies in a paragraph.
citations.quote: (iii) it compares entity frequency to the frequency of its co-occurring mentions as the weight of an entity appearing in a specific paragraph, normalized by the sum of the frequencies of other entities in INLINEFORM2 .

output.answer: In ViT, the learnable class token is prepended to the patch-token sequence, and its final encoder state serves as the image representation used for classification. In DeiT's distillation-token procedure, the class branch is trained on the true label, the distillation branch on the teacher's hard predicted label, and late-fusion inference sums the two classifiers' softmax outputs.

citations.claim: ViT adds an extra learnable classification token to the sequence.
citations.quote: In order to perform classiﬁcation, we use the standard approach of adding an extra learnable “classiﬁcation token” to the sequence.

citations.claim: The class token's state at the output of the Transformer encoder serves as the image representation y.
citations.quote: whose state at the output of the Transformer encoder (z0 L) serves as the image representation y (Eq. 4).

citations.claim: DeiT's distillation token is used like the class token but targets the teacher's hard label instead of the true label; therefore the class branch uses the true label and the distillation branch uses the teacher's hard prediction.
citations.quote: This distillation token is employed in a similar fashion as the class token, except that on output of the network its objective is to reproduce the (hard) label predicted by the teacher, instead of true label.

citations.claim: DeiT's late-fusion inference adds the softmax outputs of the class and distillation classifiers.
citations.quote: Yet our referent method is the late fusion of these two separate heads, for which we add the softmax output by the two classifiers to make the prediction.

output.explanation: ViT says it adds an extra learnable “classiﬁcation token” to the sequence, and the token's encoder state “serves as the image representation y” (2010.11929v2.pdf, p. 3). DeiT says the distillation token “is employed in a similar fashion as the class token, except that on output of the network its objective is to reproduce the (hard) label predicted by the teacher, instead of true label” (2012.12877v2.pdf, p. 7), so the class branch's target is the true label and the distillation branch's target is the teacher's hard prediction. For inference, DeiT's referent method is late fusion: “we add the softmax output by the two classifiers to make the prediction” (2012.12877v2.pdf, p. 8).

output.answer: ResNet identity blocks combine the identity shortcut and residual branch by element-wise addition (y = F(x) + x). DenseNet instead concatenates the feature maps of all preceding layers in the dense block as each layer’s input. Consequently, ResNet’s addends must have equal dimensions (a projection shortcut is used when channels change), while within a dense block DenseNet’s concatenated input has k0 + k(ℓ−1) feature maps, and its architecture uses narrow layers and a growth rate k.

output.answer: In ViT the learnable class token is an extra embedding prepended to the patch sequence; its final encoder state serves as the image representation to which the classification head is attached. In DeiT's distillation-token procedure the class branch is trained on the true/ground-truth label, while the distillation branch is trained on the teacher's hard predicted label; late-fusion inference adds the softmax outputs of the two linear classifiers (class head and distillation head) to make the prediction.

citations.claim: ViT prepends a learnable class embedding to the patch sequence, and its final encoder state is the image representation used by the classification head.
citations.quote: Similar to BERT’s [class] token, we prepend a learnable embedding to the sequence of embedded patches (z0 0 = xclass), whose state at the output of the Transformer encoder (z0 L) serves as the image representation y (Eq. 4). Both during pre-training and ﬁne-tuning, a classiﬁcation head is attached to z0 L.

citations.claim: ViT uses an extra learnable classification token for classification.
citations.quote: In order to perform classiﬁcation, we use the standard approach of adding an extra learnable “classiﬁcation token” to the sequence.

citations.claim: DeiT's class token is a trainable vector appended before the first layer, passed through the transformer and linearly projected to predict the class.
citations.quote: is a trainable vector, appended to the patch tokens before the ﬁrst layer, that goes through the transformer layers, and is then projected with a linear layer to predict the class.

citations.claim: DeiT's distillation token is used like the class token, but its objective is the teacher's hard predicted label instead of the true label.
citations.quote: This distillation token is employed in a similar fashion as the class token, except that on output of the network its objective is to reproduce the (hard) label predicted by the teacher, instead of true label.

citations.claim: Late-fusion inference adds the softmax outputs of the two classifiers (class and distillation heads) to make the prediction.
citations.quote: Yet our referent method is the late fusion of these two separate heads, for which we add the softmax output by the two classiﬁers to make the prediction.

citations.claim: The class+distillation result corresponds to the late fusion of the class and distillation classifiers.
citations.quote: In the last row (class+distillation), the result correspond to the late fusion of the class and distillation classiﬁers.

output.explanation: ViT follows BERT by prepending a learnable [class] token, using its output state as the image representation y and attaching the classification head to it [1][2]. DeiT describes this same token as a trainable vector that goes through the transformer layers and is then linearly projected to predict the class [3]. Its added distillation token is used similarly but its objective is the teacher's hard label rather than the true label, so the class branch targets the true label and the distillation branch targets the teacher prediction [4]. At test time both embeddings feed separate linear classifiers, and the paper's referent late fusion adds the two softmax outputs to form the prediction [5]; Table 3 confirms that the class+distillation result corresponds to this late fusion [6].
